pages.name: What does the cue ball do?
pages.task: Two equal balls are set to ideal bouncy, so no kinetic energy is lost in the bounce. A cue ball at 2.0 m/s hits a still one dead centre. What does the cue ball do?
pages.answer: It stops, and the other ball goes on at its speed
pages.why: Each ball is an example 0.2 kg. Before the hit, the shot carries 0.2 × 2.0 = 0.4 kg m/s of momentum. It also carries ½ × 0.2 × 2.0² = 0.4 J of kinetic energy. The struck ball leaving at 2.0 m/s carries both, exactly. Rolling on together at 1.0 m/s keeps the 0.4 kg m/s but only 0.2 J. An ideal bouncy hit keeps both. So the cue ball stops dead.

pages.name: Momentum has a direction
pages.text: A ball's momentum is its mass × its velocity, in kg m/s. Call one way positive. A ball going the other way has negative momentum. A 0.2 kg ball at 2.0 m/s to the right carries +0.4 kg m/s. An equal ball at 1.5 m/s to the left carries −0.3 kg m/s. Nose to tail, the arrows total 0.1 kg m/s to the right.

pages.name: The total
pages.task: Take right as positive. A 0.4 kg ball rolls right at 2.0 m/s. A 0.2 kg ball rolls left at 3.0 m/s. What is their total momentum?
pages.why: 0.4 × 2.0 = 0.8 kg m/s to the right. 0.2 × 3.0 = 0.6 kg m/s to the left. That is −0.6 kg m/s. The total is 0.8 − 0.6 = 0.2 kg m/s, to the right.

pages.name: The total survives
pages.text: In a hit, each ball's momentum changes, but the total does not. The two balls push on each other equally hard, in opposite directions, for the same time. So the cue ball's arrow shrinks to nothing as the struck ball's grows to the same length. For a 2.0 m/s shot, the total stays 0.4 kg m/s forward.

pages.name: They stick
pages.task: A 0.4 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.2 kg ball. They stick together. How fast do they move off?
pages.why: Before the hit, 0.4 × 3.0 = 1.2 kg m/s. After it, the joined 0.6 kg carries the same 1.2 kg m/s. So it moves at 1.2 ÷ 0.6 = 2.0 m/s.

pages.name: Energy is not kept
pages.text: Kinetic energy, ½mv², is not kept the way momentum is. In a hit, some of it can go into squashing the balls and leave as heat and sound. A hit that keeps all its kinetic energy is elastic. One that loses some is inelastic. At ideal bouncy, the kinetic energy bar ends as long as it started. Towards sticky, it ends shorter. At sticky, it ends a third shorter, 1.8 J down to 1.2 J. The total momentum arrow is the same at every setting.

pages.name: Energy lost
pages.task: A 0.2 kg ball at 4.0 m/s hits an equal still ball, and they stick. How much kinetic energy is lost?
pages.why: The momentum is 0.2 × 4.0 = 0.8 kg m/s. So the joined 0.4 kg moves at 0.8 ÷ 0.4 = 2.0 m/s. Before, ½ × 0.2 × 4.0² = 1.6 J. After, ½ × 0.4 × 2.0² = 0.8 J. So 1.6 − 0.8 = 0.8 J is lost. That is half of it.

pages.name: Light into heavy
pages.text: On a bouncy enough hit, a light ball comes back off a heavier one. Its momentum is then negative. So the heavy ball carries more forward momentum than the whole shot had. A 0.2 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.4 kg ball. The light ball comes back at 1.0 m/s, carrying −0.2 kg m/s. The heavy ball leaves at 2.0 m/s, carrying 0.8 kg m/s. The total, 0.6 kg m/s forward, is what the shot started with.

pages.name: Bounce back
pages.task: A 0.2 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.4 kg ball. It comes back at 0.6 m/s. How fast does the 0.4 kg ball move off?
pages.why: Before, 0.2 × 3.0 = 0.6 kg m/s. After, the light ball carries 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12 kg m/s backwards. That is −0.12 kg m/s. The heavy ball must carry 0.6 + 0.12 = 0.72 kg m/s. So it moves at 0.72 ÷ 0.4 = 1.8 m/s.

pages.name: Along the line
pages.task: A 0.2 kg cue ball at 3.0 m/s hits an equal still ball off-centre. The struck ball leaves at 1.5 m/s, 60° from the cue ball's first line. How fast does the cue ball now move along that line?
pages.why: Along the line, the cue ball had 3.0 m/s. The struck ball's along part is 1.5 × cos 60° = 0.75 m/s. The masses are equal. So the cue ball keeps 3.0 − 0.75 = 2.25 m/s along the line. Its across part is 1.5 × sin 60° = 1.30 m/s. It points the other way, to cancel the struck ball's.

pages.name: The cannon
pages.task: A 96 kg cannon stands still on smooth, level ground. It fires a 4.0 kg ball at 120 m/s. How fast does the cannon roll back?
pages.why: Before firing, nothing moves. So the total is zero. The ball carries 4.0 × 120 = 480 kg m/s forward. So the cannon carries 480 kg m/s back. It moves at 480 ÷ 96 = 5.0 m/s.

pages.name: Which cannot happen?
pages.task: A 0.2 kg cue ball at 2.0 m/s hits an equal still ball dead centre. Which of these four outcomes can never happen?
pages.answer: The cue ball rolls on at 0.5 m/s, the struck ball at 1.0 m/s
pages.why: Before the hit, the total is 0.2 × 2.0 = 0.4 kg m/s. The third outcome totals 0.2 × 0.5 + 0.2 × 1.0 = 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 kg m/s. Nothing outside pushed, so the total cannot fall. That outcome cannot happen. The other three all keep 0.4 kg m/s.

pages.name: Coupling wagons
pages.task: A 30 t wagon rolls right at 2.0 m/s. A 20 t wagon rolls left at 1.0 m/s. They meet and couple. How fast do they move on together?
pages.why: 30 000 kg × 2.0 m/s = 60 000 kg m/s to the right. 20 000 kg × 1.0 m/s = 20 000 kg m/s to the left. The total is 60 000 − 20 000 = 40 000 kg m/s, to the right. Divided by 50 000 kg, that is 0.8 m/s to the right.
